newsitem.title: USA: U.S. political swings like channel surfing - Powell.
newsitem.headline: U.S. political swings like channel surfing - Powell.

text.p: Retired Gen. Colin Powell Thursday likened American voters' frequent changes of political taste to "channel surfing" -- flipping from channel to channel on a television set.
Powell, speaking at a Silicon Valley business awards dinner in San Jose, recounted that Americans had put the once-popular President George Bush out of office in 1992.

President Clinton then came in as a new Democrat with new ideas and Americans watched his presidency for two years. Not being able to "get at" Clinton in 1994 because he was not up for re-election, they "brought in the Republicans, Newt Gingrich and the Contract with America," Powell said, referring to the Republicans' taking control of Congress.

"It's now 1996. We are going through this remarkable democratic process again and in another two weeks we will know what the American people think. People ask me what I think will happen and I say I'm not sure because frankly, I think the American people are channel surfing," Powell said.
"They channel surfed in 1992 ... They did it again in 1994," he said, adding that he expected the trend to continue.
Powell, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and a Gulf War hero, said nothing about his own political ambitions.

Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole said last week that Powell would be "a star" in his administration if he defeated Clinton in next month's election. There has been speculation Powell could be named to a senior cabinet position in a Dole administration.
Powell, 59, who decided against launching his own bid for the White House, has said he would consider accepting a cabinet appointment.
Powell said the American people were not "speaking clearly to their leaders."

Voters were saying they wanted lower taxes and less government, Powell said. "But it's not clear that each and every one of us is prepared to give up what we get from the government as a result of taxes," he said.

Voters also wanted politicians to get people off welfare, Powell said, but added: "We're all on welfare. Every one of us in this room enjoys something from the government." Fiscal responsibility could only come about if everyone gave up something, Powell said.
